text_blocks.snippet: Vaccines typically contain antigens, which trigger an immune response in the body, along with other ingredients that help the vaccine work effectively and safely. These ingredients can include adjuvants to boost the immune response, preservatives to prevent contamination, stabilizers to maintain vaccine integrity, and trace amounts of materials used during the manufacturing process.

list.title: Antigens:
list.snippet: The active ingredient in a vaccine that stimulates the immune system to recognize and fight off a specific disease. Antigens can be whole weakened or inactive viruses or bacteria, parts of these organisms, or even instructions (mRNA) for the body to produce the antigen itself.

list.title: Adjuvants:
list.snippet: Substances that enhance the immune response to the antigen, allowing for a more robust and long-lasting protection.

list.title: Stabilizers:
list.snippet: Substances like gelatin, which prevent the vaccine components from breaking down during storage and transportation.

list.title: Preservatives:
list.snippet: Used in multi-dose vials to prevent contamination by bacteria or fungi, though many vaccines now come in single-dose presentations and do not require preservatives.

list.title: Trace materials:
list.snippet: Small amounts of substances used during the manufacturing process, like egg proteins or formaldehyde, that are present at very low levels in the final product.

text_blocks.snippet: Vaccines introduce antigens into the body, which the immune system recognizes as foreign invaders. This triggers the production of antibodies, which are specialized proteins that bind to and neutralize the disease-causing organism. When the body later encounters the real pathogen, the immune system can quickly respond and prevent or lessen the severity of the illness.

list.snippet: Inactivated or killed viruses: Polio, hepatitis A, rabies, and some influenza vaccines.
Weakened live viruses: Measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), rotavirus, chickenpox (varicella), and some influenza vaccines.
Virus subunits: Hepatitis B and HPV vaccines.
Aluminum salts: Adjuvants used in many vaccines.
Gelatin: A stabilizer used in some vaccines.
Thimerosal: A preservative that contains mercury, but is used in very low concentrations and is not a concern for safety, according to the FDA.
